stem: What is the primary distinguishing characteristic of a Weak Entity Set in an Entity-Relationship (ER) model?

options.text: It cannot have any attributes attached to it in the ER diagram.
It does not possess a primary key of its own and depends on an identifying strong entity set.
It can only participate in binary 1:1 relationships.
It is stored in a separate temporary file system rather than a relational table.

explanation: A weak entity set lacks a primary key and relies on an identifying relationship with a strong entity set along with a partial key (discriminator) to uniquely identify its entities.
closestDistractorExplanation: Weak entities do have attributes (including partial keys); option A is incorrect.

Referential Integrity Constraint
Domain Constraint
Key Constraint

explanation: Referential integrity guarantees that tuples referencing another relation refer to an existing tuple in that relation, or contain a NULL value if permitted.
closestDistractorExplanation: Entity integrity dictates that primary key attributes cannot contain NULL values, which applies to the primary key itself, not foreign key references.

question: Relation R has 5 tuples and Relation S has 4 tuples. R and S share a common attribute set A. What are the maximum and minimum possible number of tuples in the Natural Join (R ⋈ S)?
stem: Relation R has 5 tuples and Relation S has 4 tuples. R and S share a common attribute set A. What are the maximum and minimum possible number of tuples in the Natural Join (R ⋈ S)?

options.text: Maximum = 20, Minimum = 0
Maximum = 5, Minimum = 4
Maximum = 9, Minimum = 0
Maximum = 20, Minimum = 4

explanation: If all 5 tuples in R and 4 tuples in S have the exact same value on common attribute A, natural join degenerates to Cartesian product yielding 5 × 4 = 20 tuples. If R and S share no matching values on attribute A, the result is 0 tuples.
closestDistractorExplanation: Maximum = 5 occurs only if A is a key in both relations; here attribute A is not specified as a key.

question: Which relational algebra expression correctly represents the Division operation (R ÷ S) for relations R(A, B) and S(B)?
stem: Which relational algebra expression correctly represents the Division operation (R ÷ S) for relations R(A, B) and S(B)?

options.text: π_A(R) - π_A((π_A(R) × S) - R)
π_A(R) ⋈ π_B(S)
π_A(R × S) - R
π_A(R) - π_A(R ⋈ S)

explanation: R ÷ S finds A-values in R associated with ALL B-values in S. Expression π_A(R) - π_A((π_A(R) × S) - R) subtracts A-values that are missing at least one pair (A, B) present in S from all A-values in R.
closestDistractorExplanation: Option D computes tuples in R not matching S, which is set difference projection, not division.

stem: In standard SQL, how does COUNT(*) behave differently from COUNT(column_name)?

options.text: COUNT(*) includes NULL values and duplicate rows, whereas COUNT(column_name) ignores NULL values in that column.
COUNT(*) counts only distinct values across all columns.
COUNT(column_name) counts NULL values but ignores zeros.
COUNT(*) requires a GROUP BY clause whereas COUNT(column_name) does not.

explanation: COUNT(*) counts total rows in the result set regardless of NULL values, whereas COUNT(column_name) counts only rows where column_name is NOT NULL.
closestDistractorExplanation: Counting distinct values requires the explicit keyword COUNT(DISTINCT column_name); option B is incorrect.

question: Given table Student(ID, Name, Marks, Section). Which query correctly selects students whose marks are strictly higher than every student in Section 'B'?
stem: Given table Student(ID, Name, Marks, Section). Which query correctly selects students whose marks are strictly higher than every student in Section 'B'?

options.text: SELECT Name FROM Student WHERE Marks > ALL (SELECT Marks FROM Student WHERE Section = 'B')
SELECT Name FROM Student WHERE Marks > ANY (SELECT Marks FROM Student WHERE Section = 'B')
SELECT Name FROM Student WHERE Marks IN (SELECT MAX(Marks) FROM Student WHERE Section = 'B')
SELECT Name FROM Student WHERE Marks = SOME (SELECT Marks FROM Student WHERE Section = 'B')

explanation: The > ALL comparison operator evaluates to TRUE if the value is strictly greater than every value returned by the subquery (i.e. greater than MAX(Marks) of Section B).
closestDistractorExplanation: > ANY evaluates to TRUE if the value is greater than AT LEAST ONE student's marks in Section B, which is weaker than higher than every student.
reviewNote: ALL quantifier vs ANY quantifier semantics verified.

question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has Functional Dependencies F = {A -> B, B -> C, C -> D}. What is the attribute closure {A}+?
stem: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has Functional Dependencies F = {A -> B, B -> C, C -> D}. What is the attribute closure {A}+?

options.text: {A, B}
{A, B, C}
{A, B, C, D}

explanation: Start with {A}. A -> B adds B -> {A, B}. B -> C adds C -> {A, B, C}. C -> D adds D -> {A, B, C, D}. Since {A}+ contains all attributes of R, A is a candidate key.
closestDistractorExplanation: {A, B, C} omits D which is transitively derived via C -> D.
reviewNote: Closure calculation rechecked: A -> B -> C -> D.

question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has Functional Dependencies: F = {AB -> C, C -> D, D -> A}. Which of the following is NOT a candidate key for R?
stem: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has Functional Dependencies: F = {AB -> C, C -> D, D -> A}. Which of the following is NOT a candidate key for R?

options.text: {AB}
{BC}
{BD}
{CD}

explanation: Let's check closures: {AB}+ = {A,B,C,D} (key). {BC}+: C->D, D->A gives {B,C,D,A} (key). {BD}+: D->A gives {B,D,A}, AB->C gives {B,D,A,C} (key). {CD}+: C->D, D->A gives {C,D,A}, but cannot determine B because no FD produces B! So {CD}+ = {A,C,D} ≠ {A,B,C,D}. Hence {CD} is NOT a candidate key.
closestDistractorExplanation: {BC} IS a candidate key because {BC}+ = {A,B,C,D} via C -> D -> A.
reviewNote: Candidate key closures re-verified: B is never on RHS of any FD, so B must be present in all candidate keys.

question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has FDs: F = {A -> B, B -> C, C -> D}. Candidate key is A. What is the HIGHEST normal form satisfied by R?
stem: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has FDs: F = {A -> B, B -> C, C -> D}. Candidate key is A. What is the HIGHEST normal form satisfied by R?

options.text: 1NF
2NF
3NF
BCNF

explanation: A is the single attribute primary key. 2NF: No non-prime attribute is partially dependent on a key (since A is atomic, no partial dependency exists). 3NF: For B -> C, B is not a superkey and C is not prime (transitive dependency). Thus 3NF fails. Highest NF satisfied is 2NF.
closestDistractorExplanation: 3NF fails because B -> C exhibits transitive dependency where B is not a superkey and C is not prime.
reviewNote: Normal form conditions checked against Silberschatz.

attribution: Original for IOCL Prep Hub; not an IOCL previous-year question
subject: Databases
topic: Database Normalization: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, and Decompositions
question: Relation R(A, B, C) has FDs: F = {AB -> C, C -> A}. Which statement correctly describes the normal form status of R?
stem: Relation R(A, B, C) has FDs: F = {AB -> C, C -> A}. Which statement correctly describes the normal form status of R?

options.text: R is in BCNF.
R is in 3NF but NOT in BCNF.
R is in 2NF but NOT in 3NF.
R is only in 1NF.

explanation: Candidate keys are AB and BC. Prime attributes are A, B, C. For FD C -> A: C is not a superkey, so it violates BCNF. However, RHS attribute A is prime (part of key AB), so C -> A satisfies 3NF! Thus R is in 3NF but NOT in BCNF.
closestDistractorExplanation: Claiming R is in BCNF fails because C -> A has LHS C which is not a superkey ({C}+ = {C, A} ≠ {A, B, C}).

question: Which ACID property guarantees that either all operations of a transaction complete successfully or none of them take effect (all-or-nothing execution)?
stem: Which ACID property guarantees that either all operations of a transaction complete successfully or none of them take effect (all-or-nothing execution)?

options.text: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability

explanation: Atomicity requires that all operations of a transaction are executed as a single indivisible unit of work; if any step fails, the system rolls back to the pre-transaction state.
closestDistractorExplanation: Consistency ensures the database transitions from one valid state satisfying all schema constraints to another valid state.

question: In database concurrency, what is a Dirty Read anomaly?
stem: In database concurrency, what is a Dirty Read anomaly?

options.text: Transaction T1 reads data written by uncommitted Transaction T2, and T2 subsequently aborts.
Transaction T1 reads a row twice and finds modified attribute values because T2 committed in between.
Transaction T1 re-executes a range query and discovers newly inserted tuples committed by T2.
Two transactions simultaneously overwrite the same data block without locking.

explanation: A Dirty Read occurs when a transaction reads uncommitted changes made by another transaction that later rolls back, leaving T1 with state that never officially existed in the database.
closestDistractorExplanation: Option B describes Non-Repeatable Read, and option C describes Phantom Read anomaly.

question: Basic Two-Phase Locking (2PL) protocol guarantees which schedule property, and what problem can it still suffer from?
stem: Basic Two-Phase Locking (2PL) protocol guarantees which schedule property, and what problem can it still suffer from?

options.text: Guarantees Conflict Serializability, but can suffer from Deadlocks.
Guarantees freedom from Deadlocks, but does not guarantee Conflict Serializability.
Guarantees Cascadelessness, but suffers from Dirty Reads.
Guarantees View Serializability without requiring locks.

explanation: Basic 2PL (Growing phase followed by Shrinking phase) guarantees conflict serializability. However, transactions can still enter cyclic wait states, leading to deadlocks.
closestDistractorExplanation: Basic 2PL does NOT prevent deadlocks (wait-for graph cycles can still form during the growing phase).
reviewNote: 2PL conflict serializability vs deadlock risk verified.

topic: Concurrency Control: Two-Phase Locking (2PL) and Timestamp Ordering
question: What key operational rule distinguishes Strict 2PL from Basic 2PL?
stem: What key operational rule distinguishes Strict 2PL from Basic 2PL?

options.text: Strict 2PL requires all shared (S) locks to be acquired at the very beginning of the transaction.
Strict 2PL holds all Exclusive (X) locks until the transaction terminates (Commit or Abort).
Strict 2PL eliminates the shrinking phase completely.
Strict 2PL prevents deadlocks by assigning timestamps.

explanation: Strict 2PL requires holding all exclusive locks until commit/abort time. This ensures that uncommitted writes are never read by other transactions, guaranteeing cascadeless schedules and avoiding cascading rollbacks.
closestDistractorExplanation: Rigorous 2PL holds ALL locks (both Shared and Exclusive) until commit, whereas Strict 2PL requires holding all Exclusive locks.

question: Consider Schedule S: r1(X); w2(X); r1(Y); w1(X); c1; c2. Is Schedule S conflict serializable?
stem: Consider Schedule S: r1(X); w2(X); r1(Y); w1(X); c1; c2. Is Schedule S conflict serializable?

options.text: Yes, equivalent to serial order T1 -> T2
Yes, equivalent to serial order T2 -> T1
No, because the precedence graph contains a cycle between T1 and T2
Yes, because operations on Y do not conflict

explanation: Conflicts on X: 1) r1(X) precedes w2(X) => Edge T1 -> T2. 2) w2(X) precedes w1(X) => Edge T2 -> T1. The precedence graph has edges T1 -> T2 and T2 -> T1, forming a cycle. Therefore, S is NOT conflict serializable.
closestDistractorExplanation: Option A ignores the conflicting pair w2(X) before w1(X) which creates the reverse edge T2 -> T1.

subject: Databases
topic: Serializability: Conflict & View Serializability, Precedence Graphs
question: What strict operational requirement must a schedule satisfy to be classified as a Cascadeless (Avoids Cascading Aborts) Schedule?
stem: What strict operational requirement must a schedule satisfy to be classified as a Cascadeless (Avoids Cascading Aborts) Schedule?

options.text: For every pair of transactions Ti and Tj, if Tj reads a data item previously written by Ti, the commit operation of Ti must appear BEFORE the read operation of Tj.
Transactions must commit in strict order of their start timestamps.
No transaction is permitted to write to a data item that has been read by another transaction.
If Ti aborts, Tj must also abort immediately.

explanation: A schedule avoids cascading aborts if transactions read ONLY committed data values. Thus, if Tj reads data written by Ti, Ti MUST commit before Tj performs the read.
closestDistractorExplanation: Option D describes cascading abort behavior, which is the exact problem that cascadeless schedules PREVENT, not the definition.

subject: Databases

question: Why are B+ Trees predominantly preferred over standard B-Trees for relational database disk indexing?
stem: Why are B+ Trees predominantly preferred over standard B-Trees for relational database disk indexing?

options.text: B+ Trees store all actual data pointers/records in leaf nodes and link leaves sequentially, enabling fast range scans and higher internal node fan-out.
B+ Trees consume significantly less memory because internal nodes store data records.
B+ Trees do not require rebalancing operations during insertion or deletion.
B-Trees cannot perform exact key equality searches.

explanation: In a B+ Tree, non-leaf nodes contain only search key values and child pointers, maximizing fan-out (reducing tree height). All data pointers reside in leaf nodes, which are linked together in sequential order for rapid range queries.
closestDistractorExplanation: B+ Trees DO require rebalancing (node splits and merges) just like B-Trees; option C is incorrect.

subject: Databases

question: In a B+ tree index, disk block size = 512 bytes, search key size = 10 bytes, block pointer size = 6 bytes. What is the maximum order p (maximum child pointers) of an internal node?
stem: In a B+ tree index, disk block size = 512 bytes, search key size = 10 bytes, block pointer size = 6 bytes. What is the maximum order p (maximum child pointers) of an internal node?
explanation: An internal node with order p contains p block pointers and (p - 1) search keys. Node size constraint: p * P_block + (p - 1) * K_key <= BlockSize => p * 6 + (p - 1) * 10 <= 512 => 6p + 10p - 10 <= 512 => 16p <= 522 => p <= 522 / 16 = 32.625. Since order p must be an integer, max p = 32.
closestDistractorExplanation: p = 33 would require 33 * 6 + 32 * 10 = 198 + 320 = 518 bytes, exceeding the 512-byte block capacity.

verificationSources.locator: Ch. 11 — B+ Tree Node Capacity Calculation

question: Under the Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) protocol, when MUST the log record corresponding to a data modification be written to non-volatile disk storage?
stem: Under the Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) protocol, when MUST the log record corresponding to a data modification be written to non-volatile disk storage?

options.text: BEFORE the modified dirty data block is written to persistent disk storage.
AFTER the database system performs a full system reboot.
Simultaneously using hardware atomic dual-write bus operations.
Only when the transaction issues a COMMIT statement.

explanation: WAL protocol mandates that log records describing a modification (containing old and new values) MUST be flushed to disk before the actual modified buffer block is written to disk. This ensures atomicity and undo capability.
closestDistractorExplanation: Writing log records only at COMMIT (option D) violates the STEAL buffer policy where uncommitted dirty pages can be flushed to disk before commit.

sourceLocator: p. 2 — Databases: crash recovery and deferred update
subject: Databases
topic: Transaction Processing and ACID Properties
question: In crash recovery using Deferred Update (No-Undo/Redo) policy, what actions are taken for committed transactions vs active uncommitted transactions found in the log?
stem: In crash recovery using Deferred Update (No-Undo/Redo) policy, what actions are taken for committed transactions vs active uncommitted transactions found in the log?

options.text: REDO committed transactions; NO UNDO needed for active uncommitted transactions.
UNDO committed transactions; REDO active uncommitted transactions.
UNDO both committed and uncommitted transactions.
REDO all active transactions and delete log records of committed transactions.

explanation: In Deferred Update mode, data modifications are held in log buffers and never written to disk until the transaction commits. Thus, active uncommitted transactions never altered the disk state (so no UNDO is required), while committed transactions are REDONE to guarantee durability.
closestDistractorExplanation: Immediate Update mode (with STEAL policy) requires both REDO and UNDO operations during crash recovery.
